title: The Limits of Quantum Computers for Power Flow
abstract: This letter proves realistic grid properties limit the applicability of quantum computers for power flow. Grids that split into two large regions meeting at only a few buses, common in transmission networks, force the pseudo condition number of the DC susceptance matrix to grow polynomially in the network size, and long chains of lines bridging such regions force quadratic growth, making recent empirical observations rigorous. The bounds also hold with overwhelming probability for arbitrary bounded random line susceptances. Combined with query and tomography lower bounds, this precludes end-to-end quantum advantage for DC power flow at every readout level, and these obstructions persist through AC power flow, optimal power flow, and unit commitment. All proofs are formally verified with accompanying Lean 4 source code.
summary: This work proves that inherent topological features of real power grids cause the necessary matrices for solving power flow problems to become extremely ill-conditioned. This structural limitation forces both classical and quantum computation time requirements to scale poorly with grid size, effectively precluding a general end-to-end quantum advantage for these critical engineering tasks.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quantum computers can achieve an end-to-end computational advantage over classical methods when solving large-scale power flow problems.
main_result: Structural properties of realistic electrical grids, such as graph separators and long corridors, cause the underlying mathematical matrices to become severely ill-conditioned, precluding a general quantum advantage for these tasks.
method: The analysis combines rigorous graph theory (analyzing network topology) with quantum complexity theory (query and readout bounds) to establish lower bounds on computational difficulty.
model_or_system: The model is an electrical transmission network represented by graphs $G=(V, E)$, whose core mathematical structure involves the susceptance Laplacian matrix. The problems analyzed include DC/AC Power Flow, Optimal Power Flow, and Unit Commitment.
key_observables: Pseudo condition number ($\kappa_+(B)$), which dictates the required computational resources for solving linear systems derived from network physics.
important_parameters: Network size ($n$), graph separators, corridor lengths ($\ell$), and quantum complexity bounds related to $\epsilon$ (precision).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that realistic grid topologies exhibit structural limitations like separators or corridors, and it proves the lack of advantage at *every* readout level.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by analyzing the condition number growth based on network topology (separators vs. corridors), demonstrating that this growth forces quantum query complexity to exceed classical scaling, and then generalizing these obstructions across various power flow formulations.
why_interesting: While focused on electrical engineering, the core mathematical tools—analyzing computational bottlenecks via matrix conditioning and structural graph properties—are highly relevant to understanding resource limitations in simulating complex quantum many-body systems or analyzing quantum network architectures.
